questions.enonce_markdown:
You are provided with a positively charged rod X, and two charged spheres A and B. One of the spheres is positively charged while the other is negatively charged.

(i) What is a charged material? *[1 mark]*

(ii) Describe test that you would carry out using the charged rod to identify the charges on the two spheres. *[4 marks]*

(iii) Draw the electric field pattern around the positively charged sphere. *[2 marks]*
questions.corrige_markdown:
(i) A **charged material** is a body that has a **net electric charge**, because it has **gained or lost electrons**: an excess of electrons makes it negative, a deficiency of electrons makes it positive.

(ii) **Test:** hang each sphere on an **insulating thread** (or place it on an insulating stand) so that its charge cannot leak away.

1. Bring the positively charged rod X slowly near sphere A, without touching it, and observe.
2. Repeat with sphere B.
3. The sphere that is **repelled** by the rod has charge of the **same sign as X**, so it is **positively charged**. The sphere that is **attracted** by the rod is **negatively charged**.

Repulsion is the only sure test of the sign of a charge, because a rod may also attract an uncharged body; since one sphere is positive and the other is negative, only the positive sphere is repelled.

(iii) **Field pattern (to be drawn):** draw a circle for the sphere and **straight lines drawn radially outward from the sphere**, evenly spaced, starting perpendicular to its surface, each with an **arrow pointing away from the sphere** (the field direction is the direction of the force on a positive test charge). The lines are closer together near the sphere, where the field is stronger.

questions.enonce_markdown:
Figure 5 shows a circuit diagram operating three $6\,\Omega$ bulbs connected as shown.

![fig-1](gce-ol-physics-2024-p2-officiel-cameroun_exercice_9_fig_1.png)

*Figure 5*

Calculate:

(i) the combined resistance of the resistors. *[2 marks]*

(ii) the current flowing through the circuit. *[2 marks]*

(iii) the total power dissipated by the bulbs. *[2 marks]*

(iv) state two advantages of connecting bulbs in parallel. *[2 marks]*
questions.corrige_markdown:
(i) The two $6\,\Omega$ bulbs in parallel have a combined resistance $R_p$:

$\dfrac{1}{R_p} = \dfrac{1}{6} + \dfrac{1}{6} = \dfrac{2}{6}$, so $R_p = 3\,\Omega$.

This is in series with the third $6\,\Omega$ bulb:

$R = 3 + 6 = 9\,\Omega$

**The combined resistance is $9\,\Omega$.**

(ii) $I = \dfrac{V}{R} = \dfrac{24}{9} = 2.67\,\mathrm{A}$

**The current is about $2.67\,\mathrm{A}$.**

(iii) $P = VI = 24 \times 2.67 = 64\,\mathrm{W}$

(Check: $P = \dfrac{V^2}{R} = \dfrac{24^2}{9} = 64\,\mathrm{W}$.)

**The total power dissipated is $64\,\mathrm{W}$.**

(iv) Any two of: if one bulb **fails (burns out)**, the others in parallel **stay lit**, because each branch is independent; each branch can be **switched on and off separately** with its own switch; each bulb in a parallel branch receives the **full supply voltage** (so full brightness); the **total resistance is reduced**, so more current can be drawn from the supply.

questions.enonce_markdown:
A wire has a resistance of $10\,\Omega$. A similar wire of the same material is twice as long but of the same thickness.

(i) Compare the resistances of the two wires. *[3 marks]*

(ii) State and explain one other factor which affects the resistance of the wire. *[2 marks]*
questions.corrige_markdown:
(i) For wires of the same material and the same thickness (same cross-sectional area), the resistance is **directly proportional to the length**: $R \propto l$.

The second wire is twice as long, so $R_2 = 2 \times 10 = 20\,\Omega$.

**The longer wire has twice the resistance of the first one ($20\,\Omega$ against $10\,\Omega$).** The electrons meet twice as many collisions with the atoms of the wire along the longer path.

(ii) Any one of:

- **Cross-sectional area (thickness)**: a thicker wire has a **smaller** resistance ($R \propto 1/A$), because there are more paths for the electrons to flow through.
- **Temperature**: the resistance of a metal wire **increases** when its temperature rises, because the atoms vibrate more and collide more often with the moving electrons.
- **Type of material** (resistivity): copper has a lower resistance than nichrome for the same size.

questions.enonce_markdown:
You are provided with a bar magnet, M, and two other bars, X and Y. One a bar magnet and the other a magnetic material.

(i) What is a magnet? *[1 mark]*

(ii) Describe test that you would carry out using the magnet M to identify the other bars. *[4 marks]*

(iii) Draw the magnetic field pattern around the bar magnet. *[2 marks]*
questions.corrige_markdown:
(i) A **magnet** is a body (a piece of iron, steel, cobalt or nickel, or an alloy) that **attracts magnetic materials**, produces a **magnetic field** around it and, when freely suspended, **points in the north-south direction**. It has two poles, a north pole and a south pole.

(ii) **Test:** use the magnet M, whose poles are known (north-seeking pole N marked).

1. Bring the N pole of M near one end of bar X, then near the other end of X, and observe.
2. Do the same with bar Y.
3. The bar that is **repelled by M at one of its ends** (attraction at the other end) is the **bar magnet**: **repulsion is the sure test of a magnet**.
4. The bar that is **attracted at both ends**, by either pole of M, and is never repelled, is the **magnetic material** (for example soft iron), which is only attracted by magnets.

(iii) **Field pattern (to be drawn):** draw a rectangle for the bar magnet, with N at one end and S at the other. Draw smooth **closed field lines** that **leave the north pole, curve round outside the magnet and enter the south pole** (the arrows point from N to S outside the magnet), symmetrical about the magnet. The lines are **closest together near the poles** (where the field is strongest) and never cross each other.

questions.enonce_markdown:
Figure 6 shows a simple diagram of a transformer used in a welding workshop.

![fig-2](gce-ol-physics-2024-p2-officiel-cameroun_exercice_9_fig_2.png)

*Figure 6*

Calculate:

(i) the output voltage $V_s$. *[2 marks]*

(ii) the power output if the current in the secondary circuit is $8\,A$. *[2 marks]*

(iii) the efficiency of the transformer given that the input current is $2\,A$. *[2 marks]*

(iv) state two sources of energy loses in transformers. *[2 marks]*
questions.corrige_markdown:
(i) For a transformer $\dfrac{V_s}{V_p} = \dfrac{N_s}{N_p}$, with $V_p = 240\,\mathrm{V}$, $N_p = 2000$ and $N_s = 400$:

$V_s = 240 \times \dfrac{400}{2000} = 48\,\mathrm{V}$

**The output voltage is $48\,\mathrm{V}$** (a step-down transformer).

(ii) $P_{out} = V_s I_s = 48 \times 8 = 384\,\mathrm{W}$

**The power output is $384\,\mathrm{W}$.**

(iii) $P_{in} = V_p I_p = 240 \times 2 = 480\,\mathrm{W}$

$\text{efficiency} = \dfrac{P_{out}}{P_{in}} \times 100\% = \dfrac{384}{480} \times 100\% = 80\%$

**The efficiency is $80\%$.**

(iv) Any two of:

- **Resistance of the copper windings**: heat is produced by the current in the coils ($I^2R$ loss).
- **Eddy currents** in the iron core, which heat the core (reduced by laminating the core).
- **Hysteresis**: energy lost each time the iron core is magnetised and demagnetised.
- **Flux leakage**: not all the magnetic flux of the primary links the secondary coil.

questions.enonce_markdown:
A diode is connected to the secondary coil of the transformer in figure 6.

(i) Draw two cycles of the input voltage and two cycles of the output voltage. *[3 marks]*

(ii) State and explain the function of the diode. *[2 marks]*
questions.corrige_markdown:
(i) **Graphs (to be drawn):** draw two sets of axes, voltage against time, one under the other, with the same time scale.

- **Input voltage:** a **sine wave** that alternates above and below the time axis, with **two complete cycles** (peak about $\pm 340\,\mathrm{V}$, since $240\sqrt{2} \approx 340\,\mathrm{V}$).
- **Output voltage (after the transformer and the diode):** the **positive half-cycles only**, repeated twice, with **zero** during each negative half-cycle (**half-wave rectification**). The peak is about $48\sqrt{2} \approx 68\,\mathrm{V}$ (for a diode connected the other way round, the negative half-cycles would be kept instead).

(ii) The diode **allows current to flow in one direction only** (when it is forward biased, in the positive half-cycles) and **blocks it in the other direction** (reverse biased). It therefore converts the alternating current of the secondary coil into **direct current of one direction only** (a pulsating d.c.): it acts as a **rectifier**.
